opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few reasons, and most of them aren't really about the models themselves.

The first is just that integration takes time. Even if a model is capable of doing a big chunk of some job, actually getting that capability into a workflow means someone has to figure out which tasks it's good at, build the tooling around it, connect it to the right data, and convince an organization to change how it operates. That's slow, human, institutional work. Historically, with electricity or computers, there was a long lag between the technology existing and the productivity gains showing up, because you had to redesign factories and offices around it. I expect something similar here, though probably compressed.

The second is reliability. A lot of current models can do a task well most of the time, but "most of the time" isn't good enough when an error is costly, or when you can't easily tell that an error has happened. So people end up keeping a human in the loop checking everything, which eats up much of the gain. If you could cheaply verify the outputs, or if the models were better at knowing and saying when they're uncertain, you'd unlock a lot more value from the same underlying capability. That's partly why I care about things like scalable oversight. It's a safety problem, but it's also an economic one, because trust is the bottleneck.

The third is elicitation. We often don't know how capable a model actually is until people have spent months poking at it, finding better prompts, better scaffolding, better ways to break problems down. Capabilities tend to get discovered after release, not before. So there's a sense in which the models we already have are more capable than we've measured, and the economy hasn't caught up to even what we have measured.

So when people say "the models are already good enough to transform a lot of work," I think that's roughly right. But the gap between capability and deployment is filled with genuinely hard problems: verification, trust, institutional change. Those take real effort to solve, and they're not solved by just scaling the model.

r001.rationale: The response says models’ capabilities exceed what has been measured and deployed, and that the economy has not caught up.

r002.rationale: It describes months of learning how to elicit capabilities and work to identify suitable tasks, build tooling, and adapt workflows, conveying a substantial learning curve in effective deployment.

r003.rationale: It does not predict continued improvement for roughly a decade, or say that this would happen if model capabilities stopped advancing.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I'd put it is that there's a big gap between what the models can do in principle and what they're actually doing in the economy, and most of that gap isn't about capability. It's about the surrounding work.

If you think about what it takes to deploy a model usefully in some organization, the model is a fairly small part of it. You need to figure out what the task actually is, which is often not obvious even to the people doing it. You need to get the data into a form the model can see. You need some evaluation of whether it's doing the right thing, because you can't just trust it blindly. You need to integrate it into whatever workflow or software already exists, which is usually a mess. And then you need someone to be responsible for it when it goes wrong. All of that is slow, human, organizational labor, and it scales with the number of use cases rather than with the model's intelligence.

So even if we froze the models today, I think you'd see years of continued economic growth from people just gradually working through that backlog. We've seen this before with other general technologies. Electricity took decades to show up in productivity statistics, not because the electricity wasn't good enough but because factories had to be redesigned around it.

The other piece is that the models are often already better than people realize at a given task, but nobody has checked. There's a huge amount of low-hanging fruit where the barrier is simply that someone hasn't sat down and tried the thing carefully, with good prompting and good scaffolding and some sensible checking of outputs. When people do try, they're frequently surprised.

I'd add one caveat, which is that "untapped potential" cuts both ways. The same gap means we have less information than we'd like about how these systems behave once they're deeply embedded in things that matter. So I'm somewhat glad the diffusion is slow, because it gives us time to get the safety and evaluation side in order. But in terms of the pure economics, yes, I think we're nowhere near using what already exists.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes a gap between what models can do and how much they are actually used in the economy.

r002.rationale: It describes substantial task-specific work to deploy models effectively, including figuring out tasks, preparing data, evaluating outputs, and integrating workflows, as well as careful experimentation with prompting and scaffolding.

r003.rationale: It predicts continued growth for “years,” but does not specify or clearly imply a period of roughly a decade.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a pretty large gap between what a model can do in a demonstration and what people have actually built useful workflows around. Even if you froze the models today, there would be a lot of work left in figuring out where they’re useful, connecting them to the right information and tools, and changing how organisations operate to take advantage of them.

One important obstacle is reliability. A model can do something impressive most of the time, but if you have to check every step, that can eat up a lot of the benefit. So there’s potential in making the whole system more reliable, even without making the underlying model more intelligent. You can choose tasks where errors are easy to catch, build in checks, and make it easy for a person to intervene.

And that kind of adaptation takes time. People have to experiment and discover which applications actually save work. So I wouldn’t interpret limited adoption in some areas as evidence that the models lack the capability. Some of it is that we haven’t yet worked out how to turn that capability into dependable economic value.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between what models can demonstrate and the useful workflows people have built around them, and says limited adoption does not mean the models lack capability.

r002.rationale: It says people need time to experiment and discover useful applications, but does not identify a substantial learning curve within a particular area of work.

r003.rationale: The response says there is work left even if models were frozen, but gives no prediction that this improvement could continue for roughly a decade.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a big gap between what a model can do in a demo and what people have figured out how to use it for reliably. Being able to do a task once is different from being able to slot it into a business process, handle the unusual cases, and know when you need a human to check the result.

And a lot of the work is on the human side: figuring out which tasks to delegate, giving the model the right context, and changing workflows around it. That takes time. So even if the models stopped improving, I’d expect substantial gains from learning how to use the capabilities we already have.

r001.rationale: It describes a gap between what models can do and how reliably people have learned to use them in business processes.

r002.rationale: It says effective use takes time and requires selecting tasks, providing context, and adapting workflows.

r003.rationale: It predicts further gains if models stop improving, but gives no timeframe of roughly a decade.
